title: Google Business Profile: why creating articles for your profile matters
excerpt: Publishing articles on your Google Business Profile keeps it active, answers questions before the first contact, and sends customers to your website. Here's how to set up a simple routine.
content:
Publishing articles on your Google Business Profile (formerly Google My Business) keeps the profile active, answers questions before the first contact, and sends customers straight to your website or WhatsApp. It's a free channel, seen by people who are already looking for what you sell, right when they're deciding.

Even so, most businesses create the profile, add an address and phone number, and never go back. In this article you'll learn what these posts are, why they make a difference, and how to set up a simple routine to keep your profile alive.

What are Google Business Profile articles?

They're short posts that show up inside your profile on Search and Google Maps, in the updates section. They work like a bulletin board: you can announce something new, promote an offer, share an event, or summarize a useful piece from your blog.

Each post takes text, a photo or video, and an action button, like "Learn more", "Call now", or "Book". In practice, it's a space Google gives you for free to talk to whoever is looking at your business at that exact moment.

Why does posting on your Google Business Profile help bring in customers?

People who see your profile are usually already comparing options: they searched for "dentist near me", "custom furniture store in Curitiba", or your business name. At that moment, a profile with recent posts says something no storefront photo can: the business is open, takes care of its customers, and knows what it's talking about.

Google itself explains that local results consider relevance, distance, and prominence, and recommends keeping profile information complete and up to date. Posts help with that in three ways:

  • They show activity: a profile that's been idle for months gives the impression of a business that's closed or not paying attention.
  • They add context: the text explains services, what sets you apart, and common questions using the words customers type into search.
  • They drive action: the button takes the person to your website, phone, or booking page with no extra steps.

There's also a benefit that grows every month: profile information feeds Maps, local results, and, more and more, answers generated by artificial intelligence. The clearer and more up to date your business information is, the better the chance it gets mentioned when someone asks an AI where to find your service in your city.

What's the difference between posting on your profile and writing on your website's blog?

They complement each other, and the best results come from using both together.

  • The blog article is the full content: it answers the question in depth, lives on your domain, and works for your website's SEO for a long time.
  • The profile post is the shop window: a short summary, seen by people on Google or Maps, with a button that leads to the full article.

In other words: the blog builds authority and the profile delivers that authority to people who are ready to buy. An article on "how long teeth whitening lasts", for example, becomes a 3-paragraph post on your profile with a "Learn more" button pointing to the full text on your website.

What kinds of posts does the Google Business Profile allow?

The profile offers 3 main formats, and each post allows up to 1,500 characters of text:

  • Updates: the most versatile format. Use it for tips, behind the scenes, blog article summaries, new services, and answers to frequently asked questions.
  • Offers: time-limited promotions, with fields for the valid period, coupon code, and terms.
  • Events: talks, grand openings, trade shows, and special dates, with start and end date and time.

For most businesses, updates tied to blog articles should be the backbone of the routine, because they educate customers and work all year long. Offers and events come in when there's something concrete to announce.

How often should you post and what should you write?

Consistency matters more than volume. One post a week, which means 52 a year, already puts your business ahead of most local competitors, who post rarely or never. If the week gets busy, 1 post every two weeks still keeps the profile active.

To avoid running out of topics, use the questions customers already ask on WhatsApp, over the phone, and at the counter. Every frequent question is a potential article. A few examples by industry:

  • Clinics: care before and after a procedure, when to see a specialist, what the first appointment is like.
  • Stores and manufacturers: how to choose the right product, maintenance tips, comparing materials.
  • Service providers: timelines, the steps of the job, common mistakes that make the service more expensive.

Write directly: the first sentence should already deliver what the title promises. Use the city and service name naturally, without repeating them to exhaustion, and always end with a clear invitation to take the next step.

How do you turn a blog article into a profile post?

  1. Pick the article: go for the ones that answer a question from someone close to buying.
  2. Sum it up in up to 3 short paragraphs: the main answer, one useful detail, and an invitation to read the full text.
  3. Use your own image: a real photo of your team, your work, or your product works better than a stock image.
  4. Set up the "Learn more" button pointing to the article on your website.
  5. Review before publishing: Google may reject posts with a phone number in the text, too much promotion, or suspicious links.
  6. Track the results: the profile dashboard shows views, website clicks, and calls. Repeat the topics that bring in the most contacts.

What mistakes should you avoid in your posts?

  • Posting only promotions: the profile turns into a flyer and loses the trust of people who are still researching.
  • Copying text from another website: repeated content doesn't set your business apart and weakens your authority.
  • Letting the profile go out of date: wrong hours, phone number, or address cancel out all the work you put into posts.
  • Ignoring reviews: replying to every review, good or bad, is part of the same job of showing the business is present.
  • Posting with nowhere to go: without a button or a full article on your website, you grab attention and don't make the most of the interest.

Is it worth handing off this routine?

Writing SEO articles for your website, adapting each one for your profile, and keeping up the pace every week takes time and method. For many businesses, the payoff comes precisely from turning this into a process: a content calendar, texts written for Google and AI, and publishing on the website and the profile on the same day.

faq.question: Are Google Business Profile and Google My Business the same thing?
faq.answer: Yes. Google My Business was the tool's old name, and today it's called Google Business Profile. The profile still shows up on Search and Google Maps, and posts are made in the same place.

faq.question: Does posting on the Google Business Profile cost anything?
faq.answer: No. Creating the profile and posting are free. The investment is the time it takes to produce good texts and images and keep up the pace, which is what makes the profile bring results.

faq.question: How many times a week should I post on my profile?
faq.answer: One post a week is a good pace for most local businesses. If that's not possible, post every two weeks, but stay consistent, because a profile that sits idle for months gives the impression of a business that isn't paying attention.

faq.question: Can I include a link to my website in posts?
faq.answer: Yes. Each post can have an action button, like Learn more, that leads to a page on your website. Ideally, point it to the full blog article related to the post's topic.

faq.question: Do profile posts help you show up in ChatGPT and other AIs?
faq.answer: They help indirectly. AIs and local results rely on public, well-organized information about the business. A complete, active profile, combined with articles on your website, makes it clear what the business does and where it serves, which raises the chance of it being mentioned.
